item.title: Home Printer Buying Guide: Pick the Right One
item.description: Stop overpaying for ink. Learn how to choose a home printer by real cost per page, print volume, and features—plus the mistakes to avoid.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

The last printer I bought cost me $89. Over three years, I spent $340 on ink. That’s the dirty secret of the printer industry: the machine is cheap, the ink is not. If you’re shopping for a home printer, the sticker price is the least important number on the box.

This guide walks you through what actually matters—cost per page, print volume, connection options, and the specific features worth paying for. By the end, you’ll know exactly which type of printer fits your household, and you’ll avoid the trap that catches most buyers.

Start With One Question: What Will You Actually Print?

Before comparing specs, be honest about your habits. Printer buyers fall into three rough categories:

  • The occasional printer: You print boarding passes, school forms, and the odd return label. Maybe 10–30 pages a month, mostly black and white.
  • The family workhorse: Homework, recipes, coloring pages, tax documents, the occasional photo. 50–200 pages a month, mixed color and black.
  • The side-hustler or remote worker: Contracts, shipping labels, presentations, maybe craft projects. 200+ pages a month, and reliability matters more than price.

Your category determines everything else. An occasional printer who buys a $400 color laser has wasted money. A side-hustler who buys a $60 inkjet will replace it within a year.

Inkjet vs. Laser: The Real Trade-Off

Inkjet printers

Inkjets spray microscopic droplets of liquid ink onto paper. They’re cheap upfront, compact, and excellent for color—especially photos.

The catch: ink dries out. If you print twice a month, you’ll spend more on cleaning cycles and replacement cartridges than on actual printing. Inkjets also tend to be slower and noisier.

Best for: households that print color regularly, photo enthusiasts, and anyone who needs a scanner/copier combo on a tight budget.

Laser printers

Lasers fuse powdered toner onto paper with heat. They’re faster, sharper on text, and—crucially—toner doesn’t dry out. Leave a laser printer untouched for six months and it prints the first page perfectly.

The catch: higher upfront cost, and color lasers get expensive fast. Entry-level color laser toner sets can run $200+.

Best for: high-volume black-and-white printing, anyone who prints in bursts with long gaps in between, and home offices.

Quick rule of thumb: If you print fewer than 50 pages a month and mostly in black, a monochrome laser is almost always the smarter buy. If color matters, an inkjet with cheap third-party or refillable ink is the better path.

The Number That Actually Matters: Cost Per Page

Here’s how to calculate it in two minutes. Find the cartridge’s page yield (printed on the box or the manufacturer’s site) and divide the cartridge price by that number.

Example: A black ink cartridge costs $32 and yields 200 pages. That’s 16 cents per page. Print 100 pages a month and you’re spending $16 monthly—$192 a year—on a printer you paid $70 for.

Now compare: a monochrome laser toner cartridge costs $75 and yields 1,200 pages. That’s 6 cents per page. Same volume, $72 a year.

Watch for these cost traps

  • Starter cartridges: Many new printers ship with “starter” cartridges that hold a fraction of a normal one. You’ll be buying ink within weeks.
  • Tri-color cartridges: If cyan, magenta, and yellow share one cartridge, replacing it because one color ran out wastes the other two. Look for individual color cartridges.
  • Subscription ink programs: HP Instant Ink, Canon Pixma Print Plan, and similar services can be genuinely good deals—but only if your printing volume matches the tier. Overestimate and you’re paying for pages you never print.

Features Worth Paying For (and Ones That Aren’t)

Worth it

  • Automatic duplexing (double-sided printing): Saves paper and makes documents look professional. Nearly essential for school and work printing.
  • Wi-Fi and mobile printing: Printing from your phone via AirPrint, Google Cloud Print successor apps, or the manufacturer’s app is genuinely convenient. Check that it works with your phone’s OS before buying.
  • Flatbed scanner: Even if you rarely scan, a flatbed beats a sheet-fed scanner for books, IDs, and odd-sized documents.
  • A real paper tray: Top-loading trays that hold 100+ sheets beat rear-feed slots that hold 20.

Skip it

  • Touchscreens: A small color LCD is fine. A $50 premium for a touchscreen on a home printer is money better spent on ink.
  • Photo-lab quality claims: Unless you’re printing gallery prints, a standard inkjet on good paper is plenty. Dedicated photo printers are a niche purchase.
  • Fax: You haven’t needed one since 2009.

Inkjet Refills and Third-Party Cartridges: The Honest Truth

Third-party cartridges can cut your cost per page by 50–70%. But there are real risks: some printers detect and reject them via firmware, print quality varies, and a bad cartridge can clog a printhead.

Two safer alternatives:

  1. Refillable ink tank printers (Epson EcoTank, Canon MegaTank, Brother INKvestment Tank). You pour ink from bottles. Cost per page drops to under a cent for black. Upfront cost is higher ($200–$400), but if you print 100+ pages a month, it pays for itself within a year.
  2. Manufacturer subscription plans. If your volume is predictable, these lock in low per-page costs and ship ink automatically.

If you go third-party, buy from a seller with a return policy and check your printer model’s compatibility list first.

Matching Printers to Real Households

Small apartment, light printing: A compact monochrome laser like the Brother HL-L2350DW. Around $120, 4–5 cents per page, Wi-Fi, duplexing. It’ll last years.

Family with kids: An inkjet all-in-one with individual color cartridges and a flatbed scanner. Budget $100–$150 and factor in ink costs. Tank models are worth the stretch if you print coloring pages weekly.

Remote worker or small business: A color laser all-in-one or a tank inkjet. Prioritize duplexing, a 250-sheet tray, and Ethernet support. Expect $250–$500.

Photo hobbyist: A six-ink photo inkjet. Accept that you’ll pay 30–50 cents per 4x6 print. It’s the price of quality.

Before You Check Out: A 60-Second Checklist

  • Look up the cost per page for black and color cartridges.
  • Confirm the printer supports your phone and computer operating systems.
  • Check whether cartridges are individual or combined.
  • Read reviews specifically about reliability after 6–12 months, not just unboxing impressions.
  • Measure your shelf space. Printers are bigger than they look in photos.
  • Check the return window. Printers are notorious for arriving with issues.

The Bottom Line

Buy for the ink, not the printer. A $200 tank inkjet that costs a penny a page will beat a $60 bargain printer that eats $30 cartridges every six weeks—every single time. Figure out your monthly page volume, do the two-minute cost-per-page math, and pick the machine that fits your actual habits. Your future self, the one not standing in a store aisle at 9 p.m. before a school project is due, will thank you.

item.title: Best Printer for Home Use: 2025 Buyer's Guide
item.description: Stop wasting money on the wrong printer. Compare the best home printers for documents, photos, and families, plus ink cost tips that actually save.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction

Most people buy a printer exactly once every seven years, which means every purchase feels like starting from scratch. You stand in the store aisle or scroll through endless listings, and every model claims to be “the best.” Meanwhile, the last printer you owned sat unused for months, then greeted you with a dried-up ink cartridge and a blinking error light the one time you actually needed it.

Here’s the thing: there is no single best home printer. There’s a best printer for your home. A family printing school worksheets has completely different needs than a remote worker printing contracts or a hobbyist printing 4x6 photos. This guide breaks down the categories, the real costs, and the specific models worth your money in 2025 — so you can buy once and stop thinking about it.

First, Know What You’re Actually Printing

Before comparing specs, answer three questions honestly:

  1. What do you print most? Text documents, color graphics, or photos?
  2. How often? Daily, weekly, or a few times a month?
  3. Who uses it? Just you, or kids, partners, and guests?

A quick rule of thumb: if 80% of your printing is black-and-white text, you want a laser printer. If you print photos or colorful school projects, you want an inkjet. If you print rarely, you want a printer that won’t clog when ignored — which rules out most cheap inkjets.

Inkjet vs. Laser: The Honest Breakdown

Inkjet printers

Inkjets spray tiny droplets of liquid ink onto paper. They’re affordable upfront, excellent for color and photos, and available in compact sizes. The catch is ink cost and maintenance. Cheap inkjets often ship with “starter” cartridges that run dry after 30–40 pages. And if you don’t print regularly, the printhead can clog.

Best for: photo printing, color documents, families printing a mix of everything.

Laser printers

Lasers use toner powder fused onto paper with heat. They’re faster, sharper on text, and toner doesn’t dry out — a laser can sit for six months and print perfectly on the first try. Upfront cost is higher, but cost per page is dramatically lower.

Best for: high-volume text printing, home offices, anyone who prints in bursts.

Tank printers: the hybrid worth knowing about

Inkjet tank printers (Epson EcoTank, Canon MegaTank, Brother INKvestment) use refillable reservoirs instead of cartridges. You pour ink from a bottle roughly once or twice a year. A full set of bottles costs $50–$80 and prints thousands of pages. If you print a lot of color, this category often wins on long-term cost.

The Best Home Printers by Category in 2025

Best overall for most families: Brother MFC-J1010DW

This compact inkjet all-in-one covers the basics well: print, scan, copy, fax, plus automatic two-sided printing and a flatbed scanner for homework and documents. It connects over Wi-Fi and works with Brother’s Mobile Connect app. Ink is reasonably priced, and Brother’s printheads are known for handling occasional idle periods better than some competitors. It’s not a photo-lab-quality machine, but for the 90% of households that print a mix of documents and the occasional color page, it’s the sweet spot of price and reliability.

Best budget laser: Brother HL-L2400D

If you mostly print text, this is the printer to beat. It’s a single-function monochrome laser — no scanner, no color — but it prints 30 pages per minute, handles two-sided printing automatically, and a high-yield toner cartridge delivers around 3,000 pages. Do the math: that’s roughly a penny or two per page versus 10–15 cents on a typical inkjet. It also never clogs, because there’s no liquid ink involved.

Best for photo printing: Canon Pixma G620

This is a MegaTank photo printer, meaning it uses refillable ink bottles rather than cartridges. It prints stunning 4x6 photos — around 15 seconds each — and the six-ink system produces noticeably better skin tones and gradients than standard four-color printers. The ink bottles last an absurdly long time. If you’re the person who actually prints vacation photos instead of just posting them, this earns its price.

Best for high-volume color: Epson EcoTank ET-2850

For households that print a lot of color — teachers, crafters, small business owners — the ET-2850 replaces cartridges with tanks. Epson includes enough ink in the box for thousands of pages, and replacement bottles are cheap. It scans, copies, and prints two-sided. The tradeoff: it’s slower than a laser and the photo quality is good but not Canon-Pixma good.

Best compact option: HP DeskJet 4255e

If space is tight and your printing needs are light, this small all-in-one fits on a shelf. It’s best paired with HP’s Instant Ink subscription, which mails cartridges based on your monthly page count. That subscription model is genuinely cost-effective for light printers — but read the terms, because you’re renting ink, not buying it.

The Cost Trap Nobody Warns You About

The purchase price is the smallest part of printer ownership. Here’s a real example:

  • A $79 inkjet with standard cartridges: black cartridge ~$25 for 200 pages, color ~$30 for 165 pages. Printing 50 pages a month costs roughly $15–$20 in ink monthly — more than the printer itself every few months.
  • A $120 laser with high-yield toner: ~$60 for 3,000 pages. The same 50 pages a month costs about $1.

Actionable tip: Before buying any printer, search “[printer model] cost per page” and check the price of a high-yield cartridge or toner. If the cartridge costs more than half the printer’s price, that’s a red flag. Manufacturers sometimes sell printers at a loss and make it back on ink — the classic razor-and-blades model.

Features Worth Paying For (and Ones That Aren’t)

Worth it:

  • Automatic duplex printing — cuts paper use in half and pays for itself quickly
  • Wi-Fi with mobile app support — printing from your phone is now a baseline expectation
  • Flatbed scanner — essential for documents, IDs, and school forms
  • High-yield cartridges or tanks — the single biggest money-saver

Skip it:

  • Fax capability — unless you genuinely need it, it’s dead weight
  • Touchscreen displays — nice, but you’ll use the app instead
  • Photo trays and specialty media support — only matters if you’ll actually use them
  • Extended warranties — most printers either fail in the first 90 days or last years

Setting Up Your Printer So It Actually Lasts

A few habits make a real difference:

  • Print something once a week. On inkjets, a single color page weekly keeps the printhead from drying out. Set a calendar reminder if you have to.
  • Turn it off properly. Use the power button, not the wall switch. Most printers run a brief maintenance cycle on shutdown that caps the printhead.
  • Store paper loosely. Humidity causes jams and curled pages. Keep reams sealed until use.
  • Update firmware. Manufacturers occasionally push fixes for connectivity and security issues.
  • Use genuine or reputable third-party ink. Dirt-cheap generic cartridges can clog printheads and void warranties.

The Bottom Line

Buy a monochrome laser if you print mostly text and value reliability. Buy an inkjet tank printer if you print color regularly and want low ink costs. Buy a standard inkjet only if your printing is light and you want the lowest upfront price. And whatever you choose, check the ink or toner cost before you check out — that’s where the real money lives.

One printer, chosen correctly, can serve your household for five to seven years. Spend twenty minutes on the research now and skip the frustration later.

Quick picks:

  • Families, mixed printing → Brother MFC-J1010DW
  • Text-heavy, budget-minded → Brother HL-L2400D
  • Photo lovers → Canon Pixma G620
  • High-volume color → Epson EcoTank ET-2850
  • Tiny space, light use → HP DeskJet 4255e
